title: The economics of a concert ticket
text: Concert tickets are {{1}} cheaper than the market will bear. For decades, artists have {{2}} face value below what fans would happily pay, partly from anti-greed branding and partly from calculation: a packed house of {{3}} fans spends more on T-shirts, recordings and the next tour than a sparse house of bargain hunters. The gap between face value and market value, however, does not disappear — it {{4}}. Scalpers capture it, which is why tickets appear on resale sites within minutes at three times the price, and why artists complain about a {{5}} they themselves helped to create. The industry's answer has been to recapture the gap: dynamic pricing, verified resale, platinum seats. Economists {{6}} — if fans will pay 300, charging 300 funds the artist rather than the middleman — while fans {{7}} a familiar logic: the cheap ticket was part of the covenant, proof that the band was on our side. What the dispute really {{8}} is that a concert ticket is not purely a commodity; part of its price is paid in feeling, and feelings do not follow supply curves.

gaps.explanation: 'tickets are deliberately cheaper' — intentionally; derisively = with contempt.
'artists have priced face value below…' — set the price; prize = value highly, prise = force open.
'a packed house of loyal fans' — devoted ones; leery = wary or suspicious.
'the gap does not disappear — it lingers' — remains in existence; largesse = generous giving.
'a shortage they themselves helped to create' — too few tickets for the demand; shortfall = the amount by which something falls short.
'economists approve — if fans will pay 300…' — endorse the logic; appal = horrify.
'fans reject a familiar logic' — refuse it; reflect = mirror or think deeply.
'what the dispute really shows' — demonstrates; shroud = conceal, shun = deliberately avoid.
